node.label: J. M. S. Careless
node.date_label: “Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History” 1954 · Brown of the Globe 1959–63 · “‘Limited Identities’ in Canada” 1969 · “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later” 1981 · Frontier and Metropolis 1989
node.description: A University of Toronto historian of nineteenth-century Canada and biographer of George Brown (Brown of the Globe, 1959–63). 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954) criticised the Canadian historians who had adapted Turner's frontier thesis and proposed instead the study of the metropolis, a city that organizes a wide area 'through control of communications, trade, and finance'; in that view the frontier 'is in the largest sense a dependent', though 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism'. In 1969 he took up Ramsay Cook's phrase and argued that the Canadian experience must be understood through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class' (as quoted by Buckner, 2000); a decade later he added that 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism' and that limited identities 'should not limit his own perception' (1981). Frontier and Metropolis (1989), based on his 1987 Creighton Lectures, restated both themes. In period, Donald Davis (1985) judged his metropolitan approach 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research', and Phillip Buckner (2000) rejected the view, which he attributed to Careless and Granatstein, of regionalism as 'a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: J. M. S. Careless (1919–2009); “Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History” (Canadian Historical Review, 1954); Brown of the Globe, vol. 1, The Voice of Upper Canada, 1818–1859 (1959) and vol. 2, Statesman of Confederation, 1860–1880 (1963); “‘Limited Identities’ in Canada” (Canadian Historical Review, 1969); “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later” (Manitoba History, 1981); Frontier and Metropolis: Regions, Cities, and Identities in Canada before 1914 (1989). Readings: Davis (1985); Szostak (1990); Irwin (1997); Buckner (2000).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1954 article in full (Canadian Historical Review 35:1, pp. 1–21, in an Internet Archive scan of the issue); the 1979 Jackson lecture 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' in full (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981, web text without page numbers); Davis (Urban History Review, 1985, pp. 95–113) in full; Szostak's review of Frontier and Metropolis (Journal of Economic History, 1990, pp. 499–501) in full; and Buckner (Acadiensis, 2000), pp. 4–10. The 1969 article is unread here: its wording is taken from Buckner's quotations and from Careless's own quotation of its last page in 1981. Frontier and Metropolis and Brown of the Globe are unread (catalogue records; the book's content through Szostak's review). He is not presented as the originator of either idea. In 1954 he credits metropolitanism to Lower, to Masters's Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in N. S. B. Gras, and to the Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton (pp. 16–17); Davis (1985, p. 97) notes that Lower discussed metropolitanism 'some eight years before'. He wrote in 1981 that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”' but acquired it from Ramsay Cook, so that his 1969 article 'was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea'; Cook's coinage belongs to Cook's entry. Contested in period: by W. L. Morton and S. D. Clark (both as quoted by Davis), by Davis (1985), by Szostak (1990), by Irwin (1997, abstract) and by Buckner (2000). Michael Bliss (1991–92) is not recorded as a critic of Careless: Buckner (2000, p. 9) pairs Bliss's fragmentation charge with Careless's own later worry.

proposed_edges.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. Clark's at the 1974 CHA meeting that 'it serves no useful purpose to work with such categories or concepts as metropolis and hinterland when what is metropolis can also be considered hinterland' (p. 107); both are quoted-in witnesses, not read here. Davis's own judgment: Careless, combining Gras's ecological model with the Laurentian school's elites, 'has produced a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research' (p. 102); his interpretation 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'the Gras-Careless statement of metropolitanism is weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103). Davis also reports that Careless disclaimed 'such a metropolitan “thesis”' in 1973 while keeping the 'approach' (p. 96, quoting Acadiensis 3, 1973). edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition) stays: it records the urban historians' critique at group level.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: metropolitanism ('Metropolitanism and its critics') holds him and Davis; its focus still says the 1954 article is unread, which this revision corrects (see NOTES). The same pages treat the Laurentian school (strand laurentian) as the source of the metropolitan viewpoint, but the claim is his own reframing, so the metropolitanism strand is the target.

proposed_edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, and the frontierism Canadian historians took from it, criticised as environmental determinism; the frontier recast as a dependent of the metropolis (1954)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954), read in full. He summarises Turner's thesis that 'the greatest formative influence' in American history had been 'the open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6) and judges: 'This was environmental determinism at its most forthright. The wilderness and the men it produced had made America' (p. 7). Against it he sets the metropolitan reading: the frontier's culture 'originally stems from a metropolitan community; at root, learning and ideas radiate from there—and thus is Turner answered' (p. 18); 'the frontier, far from being essentially independent and self-reliant, is in the largest sense a dependent' (p. 18); and 'the functioning of metropolitanism may do more to explain the course of Canadian history than concepts of frontierism borrowed from the United States and set forth before the significance of the modern metropolis was clear' (p. 20). 'At any rate, frontierism, along with earlier schools and approaches, has had its use and its day' (p. 21). His qualifications are kept: 'Defenders of Turner might claim that he had not proposed a frontier hypothesis as the only key to American history' (p. 7); the frontier thesis 'proper' was never 'adopted as fully or dogmatically in Canada as it was in the United States—and there, of course, it has long been the subject of qualification and criticism' (p. 1); Canadian environmentalists took over 'the general approach and mood of Turner and company ... rather than the precise frontier thesis, which received little direct application in Canada' (p. 6). He draws on American critics of Turner (Hayes, Fox, Schlesinger Jr.; pp. 7–8) and on Canadian ones (McDougall 1929, Stanley 1940; p. 10, n. 21). The critique is therefore aimed at Turner's thesis and above all at its Canadian adaptation; the Canadian historians he names sit in cdn_national_tradition and are covered by edge 1. In-period reading: Davis (1985, p. 95, read) calls the article 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'. Davis (p. 109) also quotes Careless on television saying of Turner's thesis that 'like any view of history which gets oversimplified, overpopularized, it becomes untrue; it becomes a myth' (undated, a quoted-in witness). No reply by a Turnerian historian was found or read.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: progressive ('Progressive interpretations') holds Turner with Beard and Parrington; its works field names 'Turner's frontier essay'. The edge targets only the frontier interpretation, not Beard, Parrington or the consensus half of the entry. turner_social_forces_primary is the progressive strand's existing Turner source, cited so the arrow lands on a sourced Turner text; it was not re-read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Cook's phrase 'limited identities' made a programme for Canadian history (1969), and region read through the metropolitan systems that structure it (1979–89)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The 1969 article (CHR 50:1, pp. 1–10) is unread here; its wording comes from two witnesses. Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, p. 4, read): Careless 'insisted that the “Canadian experience” must be “discerned and defined” through the “limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook”', and concluded that 'the whole may indeed be greater than the sum of its parts, producing through its internal relationships some sort of common Canadianism'. Careless himself, in 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; a lecture given in 1979; read in full, web text without page numbers), summarises the article as noting that these identities 'had tended to bulk larger for Canadians in their history than any identification with overall national patterns of values and attitudes', and quotes its p. 10: 'by pursuing a line largely of sociocultural inquiry, one may hope to uncover satisfactions in the limited identities ... which have added up to some positive balance of satisfaction with Canada itself'. The phrase is Cook's: Careless wrote that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”, but acquired it from an article by Ramsay Cook, cited in my own article — which was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea' (1981, n. 1); Buckner (p. 4) says Cook 'coined' it and Careless 'popularized' it. This edge carries Careless's programme, not the coinage. The 1981 lecture joins it to metropolitanism: regionalist historians often present 'an over-simple dichotomy' between a metropolitan central Canada and their own region, whereas 'regions are structured into metropolitan systems both within and beyond their territories'; 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism. Each is inherent in the other'. Frontier and Metropolis (1989) is unread; Rick Szostak's review (Journal of Economic History 50:2, 1990, pp. 499–501, read) reports that in it 'Cities become the foci of regional identity' and that Atlantic Canada 'develops a regional identity despite having no one dominant metropolis' (p. 500). In-period reception: the 1973 bibliography by Hann, Kealey, Kealey and Warrian opened with 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for ... a historical appreciation of the varieties of “limited identities” that constitute Canada' (as Careless quotes it in 1981; a quoted-in witness). Criticism: Buckner (2000, p. 10) answers critics who treat regional studies as, 'as Careless and Granatstein seem to believe, a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'; Robert Irwin (Journal of Canadian Studies 32:3, 1997; abstract only) argues that prairie identity 'must be understood as an autonomous layer of consciousness rather than a “limited identity” within a national consciousness'; Szostak found the book 'descriptive rather than analytical' and expected readers to be 'left unconvinced' (p. 500). Buckner (p. 5) also notes the different motives: Cook and Careless embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, Atlantic historians for other reasons. edge_805 and edge_814 stay as group-level arrows.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: limited_identities ('Cook's phrase (1967) and Careless's programme (1969)') holds Cook, Careless and Buckner and already separates coinage from programme.
proposed_edges.include_note: Coordination with the Ramsay Cook draft (folder cook, prepared in parallel; not visible when this draft was written): Cook's edge, if any, should carry the 1967 coinage; this edge carries the 1969 programme and its metropolitan revision. Both may cite cdng_cook_1967 and cdng_buckner_2000; neither should repeat the other's quotations.

proposed_edges.relationship: The metropolis–hinterland approach, taken up by Canadian urban historians in the 1970s and then contested by them (1954–85)
proposed_edges.map_label: Metropolis and hinterland in Canadian urban history, 1954–85
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own statements. The 1954 article proposes the metropolis and its hinterland as a field of study, including 'social and cultural associations' as well as economic ties (pp. 17–18), and names Masters's The Rise of Toronto as the closest application (p. 17). In 1981 he writes that 'urban history' grew within regional writing because cities 'are also centres that focus and structure regions or sub-regions about them. The interplay of city and region thus demands and has received attention', and that he had 'always sought to emphasize the reciprocal and complementary nature of the relations between the great city and the territory it dominates' (Manitoba History no. 1, web text). Davis (1985) lists his urban-history articles: 'Urban Development in Canada', Urban History Review 1 (1974), and 'Metropolis and Region', Urban History Review 3 (1979) (nn. 6, 11; unread). In-period reception, from Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), read in full: 'In the 1970s metropolitanism helped preside over the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history', and according to Artibise and Linteau (1984) the articles by Careless on metropolis and region 'marked, in some ways at least, the self-conscious beginning of urban history' in Canada (p. 96; a quoted-in witness); urban historians 'have remained the most faithful to the metropolitan concept of J.M.S. Careless, the godfather of their subdiscipline' (p. 96); Gilbert Stelter called the metropolitan thesis in 1977 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history' (p. 96, quoted). A contribution, contested within the field: Davis argues that 'there is no single metropolitan thesis' (p. 107), that Careless's approach 'has fallen into desuetude in historical circles' (p. 103), that Artibise found the metropolis/hinterland concept 'not really a theory that explain[ed] Canadian urban development' (p. 103, quoted), and that urban historians 'might do better by abandoning the metropolitan approach altogether' (abstract, p. 95). Davis also records Careless's own reserve: he would 'disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96, quoting 1973). This is a Canadian contribution; it does not claim that Dyos's or US urban history drew on Careless. edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition, critique) stays: it records the field's rejection of metropolitanism, this edge the field's use of it.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: city_hinterland ('Cities and hinterlands') holds only Cronon; it is the nearest strand. A Canadian metropolitan strand, or adding him to city_hinterland, is a release decision (see NOTES). Whether Cronon read Careless was not checked; no such link is claimed.
proposed_edges.include_note: He has no urbanhistory roster row. The editor may add one (role historian or contributor, sources cdng_careless_1954 and cdng_davis_1985) or keep the edge without a row, as for Chakrabarty's environment edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: Limited identities and his own early warning against particularism (1969, 1979–81) as the ground of the later fragmentation debate
proposed_edges.map_label: From limited identities to the fragmentation worry, 1969–81
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (lecture of 1979, Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; read in full, web text). Ten years after 1969 he sees 'a massive outpouring' of writing on regional interests, cultural discords and class disparities in which 'national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted', and says: 'I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood, when he declared “Lord, I know I prayed for rain — but this is ridiculous.”' He disclaims responsibility for the flood ('I scarcely caused the flood') and does not withdraw the concept: 'I do feel the concept has had much value, and still has'. But 'Unity in diversity' now seems rather 'diversity Unlimited', and 'limited identities remain crucial subjects for the historian's regard — but they should not limit his own perception'; 'Now the task is to cut the sight-lines through'. In-period readings: John G. Reid (Acadiensis 16:2, 1987) records that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result', an argument made in Canada by Careless (graph verification note; not re-read here). Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, read): Careless 'too had come to the conclusion that the search for limited identities had gone too far and threatened the very existence of the Canadian nation-state' (pp. 8–9, citing this lecture); 'More recently the same point has been made, somewhat crudely, by Michael Bliss and Jack Granatstein and with greater sophistication by Doug Owram' (p. 9). Buckner contests the premise, calling the 'so-called fragmentation of the historical profession' 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8). An influence as precursor, not participation: his texts predate the 1991–99 exchanges, and no debate text read here names him except Buckner's. Bliss's 1991–92 article (abstract only) does not name him; Bliss is not presented as answering him. edge_814 (cdn_regional → who_killed_debate) stays: it records regional history as the debate's ground.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: limited_identities_roots ('Roots: limited identities') holds Cook, Careless, Buckner and Reid and already notes 'the first worries about fragmentation'.
proposed_edges.include_note: Matches his precursor roster row. Drop it if reviewers judge edge_814 sufficient; the distinct claim here is that the fragmentation worry was voiced by the programme's own author in 1979, in his own words.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: The 1954 critique of the 'Environmentalist School' (Underhill, Lower, Burt and others; pp. 5–14) targets historians who sit on this same entry's roster. A critique arrow and a contribution arrow to one node would confuse the map, and he presents metropolitanism as growing out of the Laurentian school in the same entry (p. 16). The critique is recorded in edge 1's evidence note; the Turner side is edge 2.

He calls metropolitanism 'at root a socio-economic concept' (p. 17) and links it to Innis's staple studies (p. 16), but edge_797 (cdn_national_tradition → economic) carries the staple approach, and Davis (1985, p. 97) says the staples thesis 'did not become an integral part of metropolitanist thought until recently'. Szostak (1990) reviewed Frontier and Metropolis in the Journal of Economic History but judged it 'descriptive rather than analytical'; that is reception, not a contribution to economic history.

Davis (1985, pp. 97, 103–105) contrasts Careless's 'ecological' approach with the dependency-exploitation school, whose 'dean' he names as Lower and which he compares with Frank's; Careless is not a dependency writer. Davis's typology could support a comparison, but the atlas's dependency entry is Latin American and world-systems work.

The 1981 lecture counts working-class history among the studies of 'limited identities', and the 1973 bibliography by Hann, Kealey, Kealey and Warrian cites his call (quoted-in). One quoted-in sentence is too thin for an edge, and edge_814 and the Cook draft cover the link from limited identities to social history.

Brown of the Globe (1959–63) is a political biography, read for this draft only at catalogue level. No reception was read. The 1954 article uses Brown, the Globe and Toronto as an example of metropolitan leadership (p. 19), and Davis (1985, p. 101) links his metropolitanism to his research on Toronto's role in 1850s reform; that is recorded in the node, not as an edge.

There is no Cook person entry in the live graph. If the parallel Cook draft is accepted, no person-to-person edge is needed: the coinage (Cook) and the programme (Careless) sit on cdn_regional/limited_identities, and each entry says so.

Irwin (1997, abstract) proposes environment as the ground of prairie identity against the metropolitan thesis; that is a critique of Careless, not his contribution. In 1954 'environmentalism' means frontier environmentalism (pp. 5–6), not environmental history.

new_sources.title: J. M. S. Careless, “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later,” Manitoba History, no. 1 (1981).
new_sources.citation: J. M. S. Careless, “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later,” Manitoba History, no. 1 (1981). The first James A. Jackson memorial lecture. Online text, Manitoba Historical Society.

verification.note: Read in full on 2026-10-14 in the Manitoba Historical Society's online text (no page numbers; quotations are unpaginated). The editor's note says the lecture inaugurated the James A. Jackson memorial lectures and reflected on ten years since the 1969 article; the text refers to the 1978 Cook bicentennial as 'last year' and to 'the close of the 1970s', so it was given in 1979. The society's page dates the issue 1981; Buckner (2000, p. 9, n. 16) cites it as Manitoba History 1:1 (1980), p. 7. Passages used: the 1969 summary ('had tended to bulk larger ...') and the quotation of its p. 10; the farmer 'in the midst of a flood'; 'I scarcely caused the flood'; n. 1, 'I did not invent the term “limited identity”, but acquired it from an article by Ramsay Cook ... essentially a commentary on his initial idea'; the quotation from the 1973 working-class bibliography; urban history and 'the interplay of city and region'; 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism. Each is inherent in the other'; 'diversity Unlimited'; 'limited identities remain crucial subjects for the historian's regard — but they should not limit his own perception'; 'cut the sight-lines through'. n. 8 credits Cook (1977) with anticipating 'the next stage for “limited identities”'.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period self-assessment: the 1969 programme reconsidered, joined to metropolitanism, and the first warning against particularism.

cdng_careless_1954.note: Read in full (pp. 1–21) for the 1.135 person entry in the Internet Archive scan of the issue (sim_canadian-historical-review_1954-03_35_1; OCR checked against the page image for p. 16). The earlier description through Davis is superseded. Quoted: 'frontierism' named 'for want of a more precise term' and the frontier thesis 'proper' never adopted 'as fully or dogmatically in Canada' (p. 1); schools 'merely for convenience' (p. 2); 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All' (p. 5); its members and 'no tight determinism is intended' (p. 6, n. 6); Turner's 'open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6); 'environmental determinism at its most forthright' and the defenders of Turner (p. 7); 'a certain tendency to fix values' (p. 12); overvaluing native and material forces (pp. 13–14); 'a wider framework' (p. 14); the Laurentian 'metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint' and 'virtually to establish “metropolitanism”' (p. 16); the metropolis defined and the 'feudal chain of vassalage', Masters and Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31); 'the other side of the coin to frontier expansion', 'thus is Turner answered', the frontier 'a dependent' (p. 18); 'a metropolitan determinism' and the Clear Grits, Toronto and the Globe (p. 19); frontierism 'borrowed from the United States' (p. 20); 'restates old problems', 'has had its use and its day' (p. 21). Davis (1985) cites the 1967 reprint in Approaches to Canadian History, pp. 78–79.

cdng_davis_1985.note: Read in full (pp. 95–113, text and notes) for the 1.135 person entry, in the Érudit PDF. Quoted: 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); Berger's 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96; n. 1 cites Berger in Canada Since 1867, 1977, pp. 87–88); metropolitanism and 'the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history'; Artibise and Linteau (1984): 'the self-conscious beginning of urban history'; Careless 'the godfather of their subdiscipline'; Stelter (1977): 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history'; Careless (1973): 'I would disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96); five approaches, Careless's the 'ecological'; Lower 'some eight years before' (p. 97); W. L. Morton's objection, quoted from 'Canada's History and Historians' (p. 98, n. 19); Careless's own account of his debt to Gras, from a letter of 11 July 1983 (p. 101, nn. 47, 51); 'a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness', 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'fallen into desuetude', Artibise's 'not really a theory', 'weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103); S. D. Clark at the 1974 CHA meeting (p. 107); Careless on Turner on television (p. 109). The 'near-doctrinal status' remark (p. 96) is from a private letter (n. 2) and is not used.

cdng_buckner_2000.note: Pages 4–10 read for the 1.135 person entry (Érudit PDF). Added: Cook 1995 on the phrase, 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8, n. 15); Careless 'too had come to the conclusion that the search for limited identities had gone too far' (pp. 8–9, citing Manitoba History, cited as 1980, p. 7); the same point made 'somewhat crudely, by Michael Bliss and Jack Granatstein and with greater sophistication by Doug Owram' (p. 9); the 'so-called fragmentation' as 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8); regionalism treated, 'as Careless and Granatstein seem to believe', as 'a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state' (p. 10); the 1969 article reprinted in Careless at Work (1990), pp. 281–91 (p. 4, n. 2).
